questions.question: A boy drops a pebble into a still pond. Rings of ripples spread out from the splash and travel all the way to the far bank. What do the ripples carry across the pond?
questions.context: A wave carries energy from place to place, but the matter it passes through stays behind. A leaf floating on the pond is not carried to the far bank: it ends up almost exactly where it started, because the water under it mostly just moves round in small loops.
questions.grade_note: That a wave carries energy but not the matter it passes through is the opening idea of the 6th-grade waves unit (TEKS 6.8C).

questions.question: A ribbon is tied around the middle of a long rope. A girl holds one end and flicks it again and again, sending humps running along the rope to the far end. How does the ribbon move as the humps pass?
questions.answer: It rises and falls in one spot
choices: It rises and falls in one spot
It rides along the rope to the far end
It slides back and forth along the rope
It inches forward a little with each hump
questions.context: In a rope wave, each bit of rope moves at right angles to the way the wave travels, so the ribbon goes up and down while the wave runs on past it. A wave like this, with the matter moving across the wave's path, is a transverse wave.
questions.grade_note: The rope wave is the standard 6th-grade example of a transverse wave, where the medium moves at right angles to the wave.

questions.question: From the end of a pier, a girl watches waves roll across a lake. Between each high ridge of water and the next lies a low dip. What is each low dip of a wave called?
questions.context: The highest points of a wave are its crests and the lowest points are its troughs. Compressions and rarefactions are the crowded and spread-out parts of waves that push and pull along their path, such as sound.
questions.grade_note: Crest and trough are the named parts of a transverse wave in the 6th-grade waves unit (G6.P9).

questions.question: A spring toy lies stretched out across a floor. A boy pushes his end toward the far end and pulls it back, again and again. Bunches of tightly squeezed coils travel down the spring. What kind of wave is this?
questions.context: In a longitudinal wave the matter moves back and forth along the same line the wave travels, just as the coils do here. Shaken up and down instead, the same spring would carry a transverse wave, with its coils moving across the wave's path.
questions.grade_note: The pushed spring toy is the standard 6th-grade example of a longitudinal (compression) wave, set against the rope's transverse wave.

questions.question: When a drum is struck, its skin jerks out and in. Each time it moves back in, it leaves a region beside it where the particles of air are spread apart. What is such a spread-out region in a sound wave called?
questions.context: A sound wave is a string of compressions, where air particles are crowded together, and rarefactions, where they are spread apart. Crests and troughs are the high and low points of a wave such as a rope wave.
questions.grade_note: Compression and rarefaction are the named parts of a longitudinal wave in the 6th-grade waves unit (G6.P9).

questions.question: A bell rings at one end of a long school hallway, and a boy at the other end hears it. As the sound travels down the hallway, how do the particles of air in it move?
questions.answer: Back and forth, each near its own place
choices: Back and forth, each near its own place
Along the hallway, all the way to his ear
Up and down, across the sound's path
Not at all, as the sound slips past them
questions.context: Sound is a longitudinal wave: each air particle is pushed a little way along the sound's path and springs back, passing the push on to the next. The air does not flow down the hallway, and the sound does not slip through the gaps between the particles; without particles to push, there is no sound.
questions.grade_note: That sound in air is a longitudinal wave, with each particle moving back and forth while the sound moves on, is the 6th-grade case of a longitudinal wave.

questions.question: A small lamp and an electric buzzer, both switched on, sit side by side inside a sealed glass jar. A pump slowly draws the air out of the jar. The buzz grows fainter and fainter until it can barely be heard, yet the lamp shines as brightly as before. Why does the buzz fade while the light still gets out?
questions.answer: Sound needs matter to travel; light does not
choices: Sound needs matter to travel; light does not
The buzzer needs air to shake; the lamp does not
The pump sucks out the sound, but not the light
Empty space soaks up sound, but not light
questions.context: Sound is passed along by particles of matter pushing on one another, so as nearly all the air is taken away, too little matter is left to carry the buzz out of the jar, though the buzzer keeps shaking. Light needs no matter at all, which is how sunlight crosses the nearly empty space between the Sun and Earth.
questions.grade_note: That sound needs a medium and cannot cross a vacuum, while light can, is taught in 6th grade with the classic bell-jar demonstration.

questions.question: A boy lays a spring toy across a floor and shakes his end from side to side, so ripples wiggle along it. A friend shines a flashlight on the spring so the class can see it better. The ripples and the flashlight's light both travel as waves. What kind of wave is each?
questions.context: What decides the kind of wave is the way the coils move, here across the wave's path, not what the spring is made of. Light is a transverse wave too: what vibrates in it runs across the way the light travels.
questions.grade_note: G6.P9 names light as a transverse wave, and a spring carries either kind, set by the way its coils move (OpenStax).

questions.question: Scientists on a boat lower a hydrophone, a microphone built to work underwater, into the sea. It picks up the hum of a ship's engine far away. What carries the hum to the hydrophone?
choices: Air trapped in bubbles in the sea
questions.context: Sound travels through liquids and solids as well as through gases, wherever there are particles to pass the push along, and water carries it well over long distances. The waves rolling on the surface are a different kind of wave, not sound.
questions.grade_note: That sound needs a medium, and that the medium can be a liquid or a solid as well as air, is part of the 6th-grade lesson that sound needs matter to travel.

cc6b236696.why: Fact-check (uncertain): the water's loops do not quite close (Stokes drift, F21), so the leaf ends up 'almost exactly' where it started. The leaf's rising and falling is cut from the context, since the ribbon question keys 'It rises and falls in one spot'. Stem, choices and key unchanged.

9a65776596.why: Judge (medium, tell): only the key answered both halves of the question. Every choice now speaks to the buzz and the light, as the judge proposed. Fact-check (uncertain): a school jar never loses all its air and the fade is partly a coupling failure at the glass (F22), so 'The glass blocks sound once the air is gone' was defensible: replaced by 'The pump sucks out the sound, but not the light' (sound as a thing of its own, M3), as the fact-check proposed. The buzzer choice is wrong because the buzzer keeps shaking (F13). Judge (low): 'until no one can hear it' is now 'until it can barely be heard', and the context says 'nearly all the air' and 'too little matter'.

4436fd6505.why: Judge (medium) and the lead: the trumpet half re-asked 'sound is longitudinal', which the hallway question keys. Now, as the judge proposed, light is paired with the one wave fact no question asked, that a spring carries either kind (F10): a spring shaken side to side carries a transverse wave. 'Spring longitudinal, light transverse' is the trap the pushed-spring question sets. Judge (low): the context no longer uses electric and magnetic fields (8th grade), and it no longer says no matter moves in light (the bell jar's key) or that a pushed spring carries a longitudinal wave (the spring question's key).
